subject: John Cassian (St John Cassian; in the East St Cassian the Roman)
texts_on_disk: design/saints-hub/sources/people/john-cassian/ (gitignored). raw/npnf211.txt is the whole CCEL plain-text volume (NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, Rights: Public Domain); ccel-npnf211-*.txt are Gibson's prolegomena, Institutes, Conferences and On the Incarnation cut from it. newadvent-*.txt are the New Advent pages (one per book or Conference), stripped of HTML (first line = URL). dysinger-latin-*.txt are the Latin (Petschenig, CSEL) with Gibson's English from ldysinger.com. Every 'exact' below was searched by script (footnote marks removed, whitespace and dash styles folded, case ignored, trailing punctuation ignored) in the file named in 'evidence_file' and in the matching CCEL file; the result is in 'check'.

text_used.text: Cassian's quotations are word for word from Edgar C. S. Gibson's translation, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894), downloaded whole from CCEL. Gibson did not translate Institutes Book 6 or Conferences 12 and 22 (both on chastity); they are not on CCEL or New Advent. Other public-domain translations used: E. C. Richardson's Gennadius (NPNF 2nd series vol. 3, 1892); Chester D. Hartranft's Sozomen (NPNF 2nd series vol. 2, 1890); James Barmby's Gregory the Great, Letters (NPNF 2nd series vol. 12, 1895); Herbert Moore's Palladius, Dialogue on the Life of St John Chrysostom (SPCK, 1921; on tertullian.org); Boniface Verheyen's Rule of St Benedict (CCEL, marked Public Domain; Verheyen died 1923).
text_used.source: CCEL cache file https://www.ccel.org/ccel/s/schaff/npnf211/cache/npnf211.txt ('Rights: Public Domain'); New Advent revised copies (fathers/3507, 3508, 3509)
text_used.note: New Advent modernises Gibson's 'Thee/Thou/Thy' to 'You/Your' (e.g. the closing prayer of On the Incarnation). Use the CCEL wording for anything addressed to God. CHAPTER NUMBERS: New Advent and CCEL follow Gibson's numbering; the modern Latin edition (Petschenig, CSEL 13 and 17) and Ramsey's modern translations sometimes number one lower (e.g. Gibson's Institutes 8.21 is Petschenig 8.20; Gibson's Conference 2.16 is Petschenig 2.16/2.17 region). Cite Gibson's numbers, since the links go to his text. SPEAKERS: the Conferences are written as talks given by named Egyptian abbots (Moses, Isaac, Nesteros, Joseph, Chaeremon and others). Scholars disagree how much is theirs and how much Cassian's own composition (Gibson, Prolegomena chapter 1: 'it is impossible to determine with certainty how far they really represent the discourses actually spoken by the Egyptian Fathers, or how far they are the ideal compositions of Cassian himself'). A careful line says 'Abba Joseph, in Cassian's Conferences'. The Institutes and On the Incarnation are in Cassian's own voice.

born.text: About 360. The place is disputed. Gennadius of Marseilles (writing in the late 400s) calls him 'Scythian by race'. Most scholars now read that as Scythia Minor, the Dobruja in today's Romania; others, including his translator Gibson and the 1908 Catholic Encyclopedia, argued for Gaul (Provence). The OCA and the Romanian Orthodox Church say Scythia Minor.
born.source: Gennadius, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 62 ('Cassianus, Scythian by race', tr. Richardson, NPNF2-3); Orthodox Encyclopedia (Pravoslavnaya Entsiklopediya), 'Ioann Kassian Rimlyanin' (Gennadius's testimony 'decisive'; 'now considered most likely' that he was born in Scythia Minor, citing Marrou, Chadwick, Stewart, Casiday); Catholic Encyclopedia (1908), 'John Cassian' ('b. probably in Provence about 360'; Gennadius's statement 'regarded as erroneous'); Gibson, Prolegomena chapter 1 ('perhaps, a native of Provence ... impossible to speak with certainty'); OCA, 'Venerable John Cassian the Roman' ('born around 360, probably in Lesser Scythia (in Dacia Pontica)')
born.note: Plain wording that holds: 'Born about 360, probably in Scythia Minor, today's Dobruja in Romania. Some scholars have argued for Gaul.' The Episcopal Church's Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 says 'Born in Romania around 365'; basilica.ro says 365 in one place and 360 in another. The Romanian Church names a village, Casian in Constanța county (inscriptions naming 'the boundaries of the Cassians' found by Vasile Pârvan in 1912), and some Romanians name Galați: these are local claims, not evidence. Cassian himself says only that his family's land was pleasant and wooded (Conference 24, chapter 1), and that his country had no monks (Conference 24, chapter 18, per Gibson). Other old claims: born at Athens (Saint-Victor breviary, 1508), at Rome (Greek synaxaria, from Photius), in Africa (Honorius of Autun, 12th century).
born.checker 2026-09-25: Gibson dates Gennadius's book to 495; others earlier. The page now says "late 400s".

grew_up.text: In a well-off Christian family with an estate near woods. A tutor gave him a classical education, and the poems and battle stories stayed in his head for life. He had a sister. He became a monk young, with his friend Germanus.
grew_up.source: Conference 24, chapter 1 (his kinsfolk's 'piety and goodness'; the 'ancestral possession of our forefathers'; 'the recesses of the woods'); Conference 14, chapter 12 ('the efforts of my tutor'); Institutes 11, chapter 18 ('my own sister'); Conference 1, chapter 1 (Germanus his companion 'since the earliest days and commencement of our spiritual service')
grew_up.note: The OCA and basilica.ro say he first became a monk in the diocese of Tomis (Constanța) and that Germanus was his relative: no ancient source says so. Cassian says the opposite about kinship: Abba Joseph asked if they were brothers, 'and when he heard that we were united in a tie of spiritual and not carnal brotherhood' (Conference 16, chapter 1).

died.text: About 435, at Marseilles. No ancient source gives the day or the cause. Gennadius says he finished his last book and his life at Marseilles 'in the reign of Theodosius and Valentinianus'. He was still alive when Prosper attacked him, in or after 432.
died.source: Gennadius, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 62 ('made an end, both of writing and living, at Marseilles, in the reign of Theodosius and Valentinianus'); Gibson, Prolegomena chapter 1 ('Cassian was evidently still living when this attack upon him was made'; Contra Collatorem 'not earlier than 432'); Orthodox Encyclopedia ('about 435', citing Cappuyns, Olphe-Galliard, Weber, Pichery, Frank, Stewart; the date 433 from Prosper's Chronicle is now thought a later interpolation)
died.note: Nominis (French bishops' conference site) prints '+ 443' in its heading and 'vers 435' in its text; treat 443 as a slip.

buried.text: At his own monastery of St Victor in Marseilles, in the crypt. Tradition points to a marble sarcophagus there. His head and right hand were later kept in reliquaries.
buried.source: Orthodox Encyclopedia, 'Veneration in the Western Church' (buried in the crypt of the monastery church, citing Marrou 1945 and Stewart 1998; a marble sarcophagus 'by tradition' his; Pope Urban V put his head in a silver casket inscribed 'Head of St Cassian'; his right hand put in a reliquary in 1363); OCA ('His holy relics rest in an underground chapel in the Monastery of Saint Victor in Marseilles. His head and right hand are in the main church.')
buried.note: The Commons photo 'Sarco Saint Cassien.jpg' is described by its photographer as a 5th-century child's sarcophagus in the crypt; it is CC BY-SA, so not usable. The Revolution destroyed many relics in 1794; the head and some relics were returned after worship resumed in 1804 (Orthodox Encyclopedia). In October 2002 the Archbishop of Marseilles lent the head to the Romanian Church for veneration in Bucharest, Iași, Galați and some monasteries, and gave it relics (Orthodox Encyclopedia).
buried.checker 2026-09-25: The Orthodox Encyclopedia says only that the relics were kept at the monastery (head in Urban V's silver casket, right hand in a reliquary of 1363); "in the church above" is not in it. The burial in the crypt is "by tradition" there.

also_called.text: St Cassian the Roman (Greek: Όσιος Κασσιανός ο Ρωμαίος, 'the Venerable Cassian the Roman'). The Greek synaxaria usually drop 'John'.
also_called.source: saint.gr, 'Όσιος Κασσιανός ο Ρωμαίος'; Great Synaxaristes (synaxarion.gr), 'Ὁ Ὅσιος Κασσιανὸς ὁ Ρωμαῖος'
also_called.note: 'The Roman' probably means only that he wrote in Latin (Orthodox Encyclopedia, citing Stewart); Photius thought Rome was his home.

also_called.text: Venerable John Cassian the Roman (OCA); in Russian 'Prepodobny Kassian (Ioann Kassian) Rimlyanin, ieromonakh', Venerable Cassian the Roman, hieromonk.
also_called.source: OCA life page title; azbyka.ru, day page ('Преподобный Кассиа́н (Иоа́нн Кассиа́н) Римлянин, иеромонах')
also_called.note: Printed Greek Menaia call him 'confessor' (Orthodox Encyclopedia).

also_called.text: St John Cassian and Germanus 'of Dobrogea' (Romanian Orthodox Church, which keeps them together).
also_called.source: basilica.ro (Romanian Patriarchate), 'Sts. John Cassian and Germanus from Dobrogea' and 'Sfântul Ioan Casian'
also_called.note: Romanian: 'Casian Râmleanul' in old Romanian translations (basilica.ro).

also_called.text: In Russian folk belief, 'Kasyan' (Kas'ian Nemilostivyi, 'Cassian the Unmerciful'). See misquoted_or_legend.
also_called.source: First Things, 'Cassian the Unmerciful and (Unfortunately Long-Haired)', 1 March 2013, quoting Linda Ivanits, Russian Folk Belief
also_called.note: Folk name, not a church title. Ivanits's book itself was not seen.

also_called.text: The monks of Egypt called him John. Abba Theodore: 'How many, O John...'; Abba Nesteros: 'especially you, John'. Prosper calls him 'Joannes cognomento Cassianus'.
also_called.source: Institutes 5, chapter 35; Conference 14, chapter 9; Gibson, Prolegomena chapter 1 (Prosper's Chronicle)
also_called.note: Gibson thinks John may be his baptismal or monastic name. It was not given at his ordination by John Chrysostom, since the Egyptian monks already called him John.

status.text: A saint in the Orthodox Church. In the Catholic Church never formally canonised, but listed as 'saint' in the current Roman Martyrology (2004) on 23 July, marked as a local cult (Marseilles). Remembered by the Episcopal Church (USA) on 23 July.

patron_of.text: No sourced patronage found. Leave the row out.
patron_of.source: Wikidata has no patron item (people-audit.json: patronOfItems 0); no calendar or encyclopedia read names one.
patron_of.note: Romania has a seminary at Tulcea and a monastery near Târgușor named for him (Orthodox Encyclopedia), which is not a patronage.

in_art.text: In the East, an old monk with a grey pointed beard, sometimes hooded. The oldest pictures are two small 9th-century medallions in a Byzantine manuscript, the Sacra Parallela (Paris gr. 923). In the West, from the 10th century, he is shown as an author at work, sometimes young.
in_art.source: Orthodox Encyclopedia, 'Iconography' (the two Sacra Parallela medallions, fol. 30r hooded and fol. 74v bareheaded, 'with a grey, almost triangular beard, in monastic dress'; Einsiedeln codex 255, 10th century, as 'an author at work', 'shown young'; Dionysius of Fourna's painter's manual, about 1730: 'an old man with a pointed beard')
in_art.note: Checked by eye: both medallions on Gallica (BnF grec 923, views 63 and 152).
in_art.checker 2026-09-25: Orthodox Encyclopedia: "grey, almost triangular beard", hooded on fol. 30r, bareheaded on fol. 74v; the Erminia says "an old man with a pointed beard". "Long" and "often holding a scroll" are not in the source.

wrote.text: Three works survive, all in Latin: the Institutes (12 books), the Conferences (24), and On the Incarnation of the Lord, against Nestorius (7 books).
wrote.source: Gennadius, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 62 (lists all three, with the 24 Conference titles); Conferences, Preface to Part 1 ('twelve books on the Institutes'); Conference 24, chapter 1 (24 matches the 24 elders of Revelation)
wrote.note: Gennadius counts the Institutes as 'three books' plus 'eight books' on the eight faults, but the work is one set of twelve books. Short Greek abridgements of his works circulated in the East (Photius, Bibliotheca codex 197) and two are in the Philokalia (Orthodox Encyclopedia).

pronounced.note: No entry in Merriam-Webster, American Heritage or Dictionary.com (Dictionary.com redirects to 'cassia' and 'Circassian'). Collins answered 403. Only Wiktionary checked. See could_not_verify.

roles.name: Monk
roles.line: At Bethlehem, near the cave of the Nativity
roles.source: Conference 17, chapter 5 (the promise made 'in the cave where our Lord Himself shone forth'); Institutes 4, chapter 31; Conference 11, chapter 1

roles.name: Pupil of the desert
roles.line: About 15 years among the monks of Egypt
roles.source: Conference 17, chapter 30 (seven years, then a return to Scete); Gibson, Prolegomena chapter 1 (both visits 'between 380 and 400'); Nominis ('une quinzaine d'années')
roles.note: 'About 15' is an estimate from the dates; only 'seven years' is Cassian's own number. Safer line: 'Years among the monks of Egypt'.

roles.name: Deacon
roles.line: Ordained by John Chrysostom at Constantinople
roles.source: On the Incarnation, Book 7, chapter 31; Gennadius, chapter 62; Palladius, Dialogue, chapter 3
roles.note: Priest later: in Rome or in Gaul. Gennadius says 'a presbyter at Marseilles'.

roles.name: Abbot
roles.line: Founded two monasteries at Marseilles, one for men, one for women
roles.source: Gennadius, chapter 62 ('founded two monasteries, that is to say one for men and one for women, which are still standing'); Catholic Encyclopedia (about 415)
roles.note: The men's house was by the tomb of the martyr Victor, later the Abbey of St Victor.

roles.name: Writer
roles.line: Carried the desert's teaching to the Latin West
roles.source: Catholic Encyclopedia ('the first to introduce the rules of Eastern monasticism into the West'); Rule of St Benedict, chapters 42 and 73

items.text: saint.gr: 'Όταν το έτος είναι δίσεκτο εορτάζει στις 29 Φεβρουαρίου, αλλιώς στις 28 Φεβρουαρίου'. OCA lists him on 29 February (troparion page 'Commemorated on February 29') and in its 28 February lists for 2023 and 2025. The Romanian Patriarchate: 29 February in leap years; otherwise 28 February, his service sung at Compline.

items.date: 29 February (old style) in leap years, 28 February (old style) in other years; both fall on 13 March on the civil calendar
items.text: azbyka.ru: 13 March 2024 = 29 February old style, 'Прп. Кассиа́на (Иоа́нна Кассиа́на) Римлянина, иеромонаха (435)'; 13 March 2025 = 28 February old style, same entry. His day page gives 'День памяти 13 марта'.
items.source: azbyka.ru day pages for 13 March 2024 and 2025; azbyka.ru saint page
items.note: So in Russia his day never moves: always 13 March civil.

items.text: Not in the General Roman Calendar. The Roman Martyrology of 2004 lists him on 23 July, entry 5, with an asterisk: 'Massiliae in Provincia Galliae, sancti Ioannis Cassiani, presbyteri, qui duo monasteria, alterum pro viris, alterum pro mulieribus, condidit et, longo rerum monasticarum usu peritus, de Coenobiticis Institutis et Collationes Patrum scripsit ad aedificationem monachorum.' The Martyrology's own rules: an asterisk marks a particular or local cult, read only in dioceses or religious families that have it. Nominis (French bishops' conference) gives '23 juillet, Fête locale'.
items.source: Martyrologium Romanum, editio typica altera (2004), 23 July, no. 5*, and Praenotanda 29 and Instruction 11 (archive.org OCR); Nominis, 'Saint Jean Cassien'
items.note: NOT in the 1916 (Baronius-line) Roman Martyrology: its 23 July has no Cassian and its index lists only other Cassians (26 March, 5 and 13 August, 1 and 3 December). The Orthodox Encyclopedia says Baronius left him out because of the dispute over his holiness. Latin OCR accents removed above; OCR reads 'Mlassíliz 1n'.

items.text: '23 John Cassian, Monastic and Theologian, 435', with its own collects.
items.source: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, July calendar and pp. 322-323
items.note: Collect I: 'Holy God, whose beloved Son Jesus Christ didst bless the pure in heart: Grant that we, together with thy servant John Cassian and in union with his prayers...' This is a prayer to God, not to him. It is a 2022 church text (copyright), so do not print it.

items.text: Not in the Common Worship calendar.
items.source: Church of England, Common Worship calendar (text on disk from the Origen research, searched for 'Cassian': 0 matches)

items.text: Not in the LCMS commemorations or the ELCA's Evangelical Lutheran Worship calendar.
items.source: CPH/LSB commemorations list and ELW church year (texts on disk from the Origen and Basil research, searched for 'Cassian': 0 matches)

why.text: East: the oldest Greek lists (copied 1050 and 1063 in Palestine) put him on 28 February. From the 12th century the Jerusalem Typikon puts him on 29 February, and printed Menaia fixed that date. He is the only saint with a service on 29 February, so in other years it moves to 28 February. West: 23 July was Marseilles's own feast, kept with an octave at St Victor.
why.source: Orthodox Encyclopedia, 'Veneration in the Eastern Church' and 'in the Western Church'; Catholic Encyclopedia ('At Marseilles his feast is celebrated, with an octave, 23 July')
why.note: Gibson (1894) doubted that the Cassian of 29 February is our Cassian, because the Horologion calls that Cassian a former soldier; he suggested the Cassian of the Roman Martyrology's 13 August. The Orthodox churches' own lives (OCA, synaxaria, Romanian Patriarchate) clearly mean John Cassian of Marseilles. Print the churches' view; the old doubt can go in a note.

numbers.source: saint.gr; Orthodox Encyclopedia (the only saint with a service on 29 February)
numbers.note: A fun, true number. Keep the second line so no one thinks he goes uncelebrated.

lines: They had promised to be back soon
numbers.source: Conference 17, chapter 30 ('when seven years were over we were very glad to fulfil it')

lines: One for each elder in Revelation 4
numbers.source: Conference 24, chapter 1; Gennadius, chapter 62; New Advent index of the Conferences (15 named abbots: Moses, Paphnutius, Daniel, Serapion, Theodore, Serenus, Isaac, Chaeremon, Nesteros, Joseph, Piamun, John, Pinufius, Theonas, Abraham)
numbers.note: 15 is our count from the titles (Conferences 12 and 22, not on New Advent, are by Chaeremon and Theonas, already counted).

numbers.source: Conference 11, chapter 4 ('he had passed the hundredth year of his life')

lines: One for men, one for women

numbers.source: Rule of St Benedict, chapter 42 (Verheyen): 'let one read the Conferences or the Lives of the Fathers'; 'when the four or five pages have been read'
numbers.note: Benedict does not name Cassian; 'the Conferences' ('Collationes') is the title of Cassian's book, and chapter 73 pairs 'the collations of the Fathers, and their institutes'. Gibson and the Catholic Encyclopedia read these as Cassian's works.

traits.title: honest about his temper
traits.text: Living alone as a hermit, he found he still lost his temper: at his pen, at his blunt penknife, at a flint too slow to spark. His lesson: going off alone does not cure a temper.
traits.exact: For we recollect that when we were living in solitude a feeling of irritation would creep over us against our pen because it was too large or too small; against our penknife when it cut badly and with a blunt edge what we wanted cut
traits.note: The flint: Gibson's English says 'a spark of fire flashed out', which garbles the Latin 'tardius scintilla ignis emicuit' (the spark came out too slowly). Say 'a flint slow to spark'; do not quote Gibson's flint clause.

traits.title: bookish, and it bothered him
traits.text: He told Abba Nesteros that the poems and battle stories of his schooling came back to him even while he prayed.
traits.exact: my mind is filled with those songs of the poets so that even at the hour of prayer it is thinking about those trifling fables, and the stories of battles with which from its earliest infancy it was stored by its childish lessons
traits.note: Nesteros's answer: fill the mind with Scripture with the same zeal (chapter 13).

traits.title: a friend for life
traits.text: Germanus was with him from his first days as a monk, in Bethlehem, in the desert, in Constantinople and in Rome.
traits.exact: everybody would say that a single heart and soul existed in our two bodies
traits.note: Germanus is not heard of after Rome (Catholic Encyclopedia).

traits.title: able to laugh at himself
traits.text: He passes on an old saying that a monk should run from women and bishops, and admits he managed neither: his sister kept in touch, and a bishop ordained him.
traits.exact: though I cannot produce it without shame on my own part, since I could not avoid my own sister, nor escape the hands of the bishop
traits.note: The bishop was John Chrysostom (On the Incarnation 7.31).

traits.title: gave the credit away
traits.text: At the end of his book of talks on promises, he tells readers where the good parts came from.
traits.exact: whatever in it pleases them belongs to the fathers, and whatever they dislike is all our own
traits.note: Latin (Petschenig, via Dysinger): 'ut quidquid in eis placuerit patrum, nostrum uero sciant esse quod displicet'.

traits.title: loyal to his teacher
traits.text: More than twenty-five years after Chrysostom's exile, he still called himself his disciple, and said his own book was really his teacher's.
traits.exact: for it was he who taught me what I have written

life_moments.title: A famous abbot in their cell
life_moments.text: Cassian and Germanus became monks near the cave of the Nativity. One day a new novice was put in their cell. He was Pinufius, a famous Egyptian abbot hiding from praise. He was found out and taken home in honour. Years later he welcomed them in Egypt.
life_moments.source: Conferences, Conference 20, chapters 1 and 2; Institutes, Book 4, chapters 30 and 31
life_moments.note: 'About 380': Orthodox Encyclopedia (Stewart); others say 382-383. Exact: 'he was received as a beginner and a novice in the house of that monastery in which we were living, and was charged by the Abbot to stop in our cell'. (Checked, Conference 20, chapter 1.)

life_moments.title: Fasts broken for guests
life_moments.text: In Palestine they had been taught never to eat before the set hour. In Egypt, wherever they went, the old monks broke their fast to eat with them. One elder explained that he could fast any day, but he could not keep them with him always.
life_moments.note: Exact: 'The opportunity for fasting is always with me. But as I am going to conduct you on your way, I cannot always keep you with me.'

life_moments.title: A cell given away twice
life_moments.text: Abba Archebius pretended he was leaving and gave them his cell with everything in it. Then he came back and built himself another. When more monks came, he did it again, and built a third.
life_moments.checker 2026-09-25: Institutes 5.37: "he left the place for a few days ... and after this returned, and with the utmost labour built another cell". Nothing says "quietly".

life_moments.title: The broken promise
life_moments.text: They had sworn to their abbot at Bethlehem to come back soon. In Egypt they lay awake, torn. Abba Joseph taught them that a rash promise may be broken. They stayed seven years. Then they went back, made peace with their elders, and returned to Egypt with their blessing.
life_moments.note: Checked (Conference 17, chapter 8, both texts): 'nor need we take it as a failure in consistency, but as a correction of rashness, whenever a promise that was faulty is corrected'.

life_moments.title: Caught asleep
life_moments.text: Late one night old Abba Theodore walked into young Cassian's cell to see what he was doing. He found him lying down to rest, sighed, and called him by name.
life_moments.quote: How many, O John, are at this hour communing with God, and embracing Him, and detaining Him with them, while you are deprived of so great light, enfeebled as you are with lazy sleep!
life_moments.note: Cassian calls himself 'an unformed anchorite as I was'.

life_moments.title: A fall they saw
life_moments.text: They saw old Heron, fifty years a hermit, destroyed. He would not break his fast even at Easter. At last he obeyed a voice he took for an angel's and threw himself down a well. Abba Moses used it to teach them discretion.
life_moments.note: Moses: 'remember what you lately saw happen before your very eyes'. Checked: he 'cast himself down a well, so deep that the eye could not pierce its depths', in the dead of night (same chapter). Fifty years: 'a man whom we remember to have lived for fifty years in this desert'.

life_moments.title: They have taken away my God
life_moments.text: The bishop of Alexandria sent a letter teaching that God has no body. Most of Egypt's monks were furious. Old Serapion was persuaded, but then he could not pray. He threw himself down and wept. Cassian was there.
life_moments.quote: They have taken away my God from me, and I have now none to lay hold of; and whom to worship and address I know not.
life_moments.note: 399: Gibson, Prolegomena ('the letters of Theophilus in 399'). Paphnutius, the priest of Cassian's own congregation, was the only one who let the letter be read (chapter 2).
life_moments.checker 2026-09-25: Conference 10.2: "almost all the body of monks residing in the whole province of Egypt".

life_moments.title: Chrysostom's deacon
life_moments.text: Leaving Egypt, he came to Constantinople. The bishop, John Chrysostom, ordained him a deacon. When enemies drove Chrysostom out in 404, the church's gold, silver and clothing were deposited with the city's officials, who were the witnesses, and took a receipt, to clear their bishop of charges.
life_moments.source: On the Incarnation, Book 7, chapter 31; Palladius, Dialogue, chapter 3
life_moments.note: That Cassian was 'in charge of the treasury' is Gibson's and the Catholic Encyclopedia's inference from the receipt. Palladius says only that they deposited the valuables and produced the receipt.
life_moments.checker 2026-09-25: Palladius, Dialogue 3: "deposited with the magistrates, as witnesses to the deed, namely, Studius the city prefect ... valuables in gold, silver, and clothing". The officials were the witnesses; the word is "clothing".

life_moments.title: The appeal to the Pope
life_moments.text: With Germanus he carried the letter of Chrysostom's clergy to Pope Innocent I. The Pope's reply to Constantinople names them as its bearers.
life_moments.quote: From the letters of your love that you forwarded to me through Germanus, the presbyter, and Cassianus, the deacon, I have learned, with anxious solicitude, the scenes of evil which you have placed before our eyes.
life_moments.source: Sozomen, Church History, Book 8, chapter 26 (Innocent's letter); Palladius, Dialogue, chapter 3
life_moments.note: Innocent's letter, tr. Hartranft, NPNF2-2 (1890). The appeal failed; Chrysostom died in exile in 407.

life_moments.title: Two monasteries
life_moments.text: Nothing is known of him for about ten years. Then he is at Marseilles. He founded a monastery for men by the tomb of the martyr Victor, and one for women. Gennadius says both were still standing in his day.
life_moments.source: Gennadius, chapter 62; Catholic Encyclopedia ('for the next decade or more, nothing is known'; 'About 415 he was at Marseilles')

life_moments.title: The two great books
life_moments.text: Bishop Castor of Apt wanted a monastery run the Egyptian way. So Cassian wrote the Institutes, on the monk's outward life and the eight chief faults. Then came the Conferences, the desert abbots' talks, for bishops and monks of Provence, including Honoratus of Lérins.
life_moments.source: Institutes, Preface; Conferences, Prefaces to Parts 1, 2 and 3; Gibson, Prolegomena chapter 1 (dates)
life_moments.note: Gibson: Institutes 419-426, Conferences 426-428. The OCA says 417-419 for the Institutes; the Orthodox Encyclopedia 420-424.

life_moments.title: A last book, for Leo
life_moments.text: He had meant to fall silent. But Leo, archdeacon of Rome and later Pope Leo the Great, asked him to answer Nestorius, who denied that Mary is the Mother of God. He wrote seven books, fast, before the Council of Ephesus.
life_moments.source: On the Incarnation, Preface; Gennadius, chapter 62; Gibson, Prolegomena chapter 1
life_moments.note: Exact (Preface): 'I had contemplated and almost determined on taking refuge in silence'. (Checked in CCEL and New Advent 35091.)

life_moments.title: Attacked, and silent
life_moments.text: Prosper of Aquitaine, a champion of Augustine, wrote a book against his thirteenth Conference. Prosper never named him. No reply by Cassian is known. It is the last thing we know of his life.
life_moments.note: Gibson: Prosper 'merely speaks of him as a man of priestly rank who surpassed all his companions in power of arguing' (Gibson's paraphrase, not Prosper's words).

miracles.text: None recorded of Cassian himself. No ancient source (Gennadius, Palladius, Sozomen, Gregory the Great, Cassiodorus) tells of a miracle by him. Leave the section out, or use an extra section on what he thought of miracles.
miracles.source: Gennadius 62 and 85; Palladius, Dialogue 3; Sozomen 8.26; Gregory, Letters 7.12; Orthodox Encyclopedia ('Veneration')
miracles.note: Later: in 1652 J.-B. Guesnay, defending his holiness, 'collected information about the saint's miracles' (Orthodox Encyclopedia); not seen. Cassian does record other monks' wonders: Macarius raising a dead man to silence a heretic (Conference 15, chapter 3), Abraham's healings (15.4-5), and a burning lamp and sulphur smell when young Serapion confessed a stolen biscuit (Conference 2, chapter 11). His own teaching puts them second.

his_view.exact: it is a greater miracle to root out from one's own flesh the incentives to wantonness than to cast out unclean spirits from the bodies of others, and it is a grander sign to restrain the fierce passions of anger by the virtue of patience than to command the powers of the air

And so we have never found that those works and signs were affected by our fathers: nay, rather when they did possess them by the grace of the Holy Spirit they would never use them, unless perhaps extreme and unavoidable necessity drove them to do so.

framing.text: Much of the Conferences is spoken by the abbots he met. The Institutes and On the Incarnation are in his own voice. Each line below says whose voice it is.

feature.exact: Wherefore this is an old maxim of the Fathers that is still current — though I cannot produce it without shame on my own part, since I could not avoid my own sister, nor escape the hands of the bishop — viz., that a monk ought by all means to fly from women and bishops.
feature.display: This is an old maxim of the Fathers that is still current (though I cannot produce it without shame on my own part, since I could not avoid my own sister, nor escape the hands of the bishop): that a monk ought by all means to fly from women and bishops.
feature.ctx: He passes on a desert saying against being pulled out of solitude, and owns that he failed on both counts. In Latin, {la|omnimodis monachum fugere debere mulieres et episcopos}.
feature.latin_source: Petschenig, CSEL 17, via ldysinger.com (dysinger-latin-inst-11.txt): 'omnimodis monachum fugere debere mulieres et episcopos'
feature.note: The 'display' drops 'Wherefore' and 'viz.,' and turns the dashes into brackets: if the page must be word for word, print the 'exact' instead (the dashes are Gibson's). Alternative feature, fully his own and gentler: 'whatever in it pleases them belongs to the fathers, and whatever they dislike is all our own' (Conference 17, chapter 30; Latin 'quidquid in eis placuerit patrum, nostrum uero sciant esse quod displicet').

check.note: CCEL prints 'current,--though ... bishop--viz.,' (no spaces around the dashes); New Advent 'current — though ... bishop — viz.,'. Same words; the checker's whitespace rule is why found_ccel is false.

lines.exact: For we recollect that when we were living in solitude a feeling of irritation would creep over us against our pen because it was too large or too small; against our penknife when it cut badly and with a blunt edge what we wanted cut
lines.ctx: His own confession, in his book on anger. The site's hook comes from it.

lines.exact: For the end and aim of patience consists, not in being angry with a good reason, but in not being angry at all.
lines.ctx: Arguing that 'without a cause' in Matthew 5:22 was added by copyists who wanted to keep their anger.

lines.exact: frequently gazes up at the sun, as if it was too slow in setting
lines.ctx: His picture of acedia, the 'noonday demon': the restless monk who cannot stay put.

lines.exact: a monk who works is attacked by but one devil; but an idler is tormented by countless spirits.
lines.ctx: A saying he says was 'handed down from the old fathers in Egypt'.
lines.voice: a desert saying he passes on

lines.exact: O God, make speed to save me: O Lord, make haste to help me
lines.ctx: The one-line prayer Abba Isaac taught them to repeat all day (Psalm 70:1). In Latin, 'Deus in adiutorium meum intende: Domine ad adiuvandum me festina'. It became the opening line of the Western daily offices.
lines.note: Petschenig's Latin (Dysinger) reads 'domine ad adiuuandum mihi festina' ('mihi', not the Vulgate's 'me'). 'Opening of every office' is the group research's claim: well known, but not checked here.

lines.exact: The end of our profession indeed, as I said, is the kingdom of God or the kingdom of heaven: but the immediate aim or goal, is purity of heart
lines.ctx: Abba Moses's first talk: the goal a monk steers by.

lines.exact: discretion is the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator
For a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered
lines.ctx: Abba Moses on telling a trusted elder your thoughts.

lines.exact: whatever in it pleases them belongs to the fathers, and whatever they dislike is all our own
It makes no difference whether gold plates, or lead, or what metal you please, are placed over our eyelids, the value of the metal makes no difference in our blindness.

misquoted_or_legend.truth: The word did not exist until about 1590 to 1600, over a thousand years later. In his day his critics called his school 'relics of the Pelagians'. He wrote against Pelagius himself. What is fair: his thirteenth Conference says a good will can sometimes begin in us, and the Council of Orange (529) rejected that view.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: The most recent investigations show that the word was coined between 1590 and 1600 in connexion with Molina's doctrine of grace
misquoted_or_legend.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1912), 'Semipelagianism'; On the Incarnation, Book 1 (against Pelagianism)

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He mocked Augustine, calling him 'Cicero': grace is defended less well 'by ... the eloquence of Cicero (i.e. Augustine)' than by the desert monks.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: A loose paraphrase with an added gloss. Cassian's real words say the old fathers did not receive the faith 'through dialectical syllogisms or the eloquence of a Cicero'. He names no one. The '(i.e. Augustine)' is the OCA's. On the Incarnation does cite Augustine, but as plain 'priest of Hippo', with none of the praise he gives the others.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: they did not receive it in a worldly spirit through dialectical syllogisms or the eloquence of a Cicero
misquoted_or_legend.source: Institutes, Book 12, chapter 19; OCA life (the paraphrase, repeated by basilica.ro and azbyka.ru); On the Incarnation, Book 7, chapter 27; Gibson's note 611
misquoted_or_legend.note: Many readers do take the chapter as aimed at Augustine's school; say 'some read it so', not that he said it.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: 'The letter teaches what happened; allegory, what to believe; the moral sense, what to do; anagogy, where you are heading' is Cassian's.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: A medieval scholastic rhyme ('Littera gesta docet...'). Cassian's own passage is Abba Nesteros's 'one and the same Jerusalem' read in four senses.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: so that one and the same Jerusalem can be taken in four senses
misquoted_or_legend.source: Conference 14, chapter 8; Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Biblical Exegesis' (the distich 'expressed by the Scholastics')
misquoted_or_legend.note: The usual attribution of the rhyme to Augustine of Dacia (13th century) was not checked.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: 'A monk who works is tempted by one devil; an idle one by a legion' is Cassian's own saying.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: He gives it as a saying 'handed down from the old fathers in Egypt'.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: Whence this saying has been handed down from the old fathers in Egypt

misquoted_or_legend.claim: His feast falls only on 29 February because he refused to help a peasant pull his cart out of the mud, while St Nicholas helped.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: A Russian folk tale, not church teaching. In it Kasyan will not dirty his robe, Nicholas helps, and God gives Nicholas two feasts a year and Kasyan one every four. Folk belief made his day unlucky. The church date comes from old calendars (see feast_days.why).
misquoted_or_legend.exact: As a result, God rewards Nicholas with two feast days per year, and punishes Cassian by granting him only one every four years.
misquoted_or_legend.source: First Things (2013), quoting Linda Ivanits, Russian Folk Belief

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He was born in Romania (or at Athens, or at Rome).
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Only Gennadius's 'Scythian by race' is ancient. Scythia Minor (today's Dobruja) is the likeliest reading, but it is a reading. 'Athens' is from a 1508 breviary at St Victor; 'Rome' from the Greek synaxaria, following Photius.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Gennadius 62; Orthodox Encyclopedia; Gibson, Prolegomena chapter 1
misquoted_or_legend.note: The Episcopal LFF 2022 says 'Born in Romania around 365'.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He was treasurer of Constantinople's cathedral.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: An inference. Palladius says only that Cassian and Germanus handed the church's valuables to the officials before witnesses and brought the receipt to Rome.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: They also presented a receipt, showing that they had deposited with the magistrates
misquoted_or_legend.source: Palladius, Dialogue, chapter 3 (Moore, 1921); Gibson, Prolegomena ('put in charge of the treasury'); Catholic Encyclopedia ('placed in his charge the treasures of his cathedral')
misquoted_or_legend.note: Low priority; include only if the page says 'treasurer'.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He ruled 5,000 monks at St Victor, and brought relics of the Holy Innocents from Bethlehem.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Both are 11th-century claims from St Victor's own charters and a Life of its abbot Isarn, when the abbey was stressing its antiquity. Gennadius says only that he founded two monasteries.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Orthodox Encyclopedia, 'Veneration in the Western Church' (charter of 1060: 'five thousand monks'; Vita S. Ysarni); Gennadius 62
misquoted_or_legend.note: No English quotation; our summary of a Russian source.

where_he_stood.text: Four of his 11 recorded positions show a line (seven are hidden: quiet, learning, alone, calm, miracles, calling, pure). Each shown line was found word for word at the place given, in CCEL and New Advent. Values from site/src/data/which-early-christian.json (people.cassian.cells).

rows.statement: Anger at real wrongdoing can be a good thing.
rows.line: For the end and aim of patience consists, not in being angry with a good reason, but in not being angry at all.
rows.speaker: Cassian himself
rows.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11 (1894)
rows.note: In Petschenig's Latin numbering this is 8.20.

rows.statement: Lying can be the right thing to do if it protects someone.
rows.line: But if we prefer what is for another's advantage to our own good, and satisfy the demands of the Apostle, we shall certainly have to put up with the necessity of lying.
rows.speaker: Abba Joseph, in Cassian's Conferences
rows.note: Is it Cassian's view? Gibson's footnote to 17.30: 'In this last chapter Cassian certainly makes his own the sentiments of Abbot Joseph on the permissibility of lying; and is therefore not unreasonably attacked for the teaching of this Conference by Prosper'. So +2 holds, but the page should name Joseph as the speaker.

rows.statement: Your body is a friend to look after, not an enemy to fight.
rows.line: For excess of fasting and gluttony come to the same thing, and an unlimited continuance of vigils is equally injurious to a monk as the torpor of a deep sleep.
rows.speaker: Abba Moses, in Cassian's Conferences
rows.note: The site's line ends with a full stop; Gibson has a colon ('deep sleep:'). Harmless, but note it if the page claims exact punctuation.

rows.statement: In many Bible stories, the deeper meaning matters more than the history.
rows.line: But as the renewal of our soul grows by means of this study, Scripture also will begin to put on a new face, and the beauty of the holier meanings will somehow grow with our growth.
rows.speaker: Abba Nesteros, in Cassian's Conferences

friends_family_rivals.name: Germanus
friends_family_rivals.text: His companion from his first days as a monk to Rome; older than Cassian, and a priest by 404. Not heard of after Rome. The Romanian Church canonised him in 1992 and keeps him with Cassian.
friends_family_rivals.source: Conference 1.1; Conference 16.1; Palladius, Dialogue 3; Catholic Encyclopedia ('some years his senior'; 'From this time Germanus is no more heard of'); Orthodox Encyclopedia (1992)

friends_family_rivals.name: His sister
friends_family_rivals.text: Unnamed. He says he could not avoid her. Later scholars think she became a nun in his women's house at Marseilles, but no source says so.

friends_family_rivals.name: John Chrysostom
friends_family_rivals.text: Ordained him deacon at Constantinople. Cassian called him 'a marvel of faith and purity' and said he had taught him what he wrote.

friends_family_rivals.name: Pinufius
friends_family_rivals.text: A famous Egyptian abbot who hid as a novice in their cell at Bethlehem, then hosted them in Egypt.

friends_family_rivals.name: Abba Moses, Abba Isaac, Abba Nesteros, Abba Joseph, Abba Chaeremon and others
friends_family_rivals.text: The desert elders whose talks fill the Conferences; 15 are named.

friends_family_rivals.name: Pope Innocent I
friends_family_rivals.text: Received the letter Cassian carried from Chrysostom's clergy, and named him in his reply.

friends_family_rivals.name: Leo the Great
friends_family_rivals.text: As archdeacon of Rome he asked Cassian to write against Nestorius. Cassian calls him 'ornament that you are of the Roman Church and sacred ministry'.

friends_family_rivals.name: Castor of Apt
friends_family_rivals.rel: bishop who asked for the Institutes
friends_family_rivals.text: Wanted a monastery in his diocese run on Egyptian lines; the Institutes are addressed to him. He died before the Conferences were done.
friends_family_rivals.source: Institutes, Preface; Conferences, Preface to Part 1

friends_family_rivals.name: Honoratus of Lérins and Eucherius of Lyons
friends_family_rivals.text: Monks of Lérins, later bishops; he dedicated Conferences 11 to 17 to them. Eucherius later made a short version of his works.

friends_family_rivals.name: Prosper of Aquitaine
friends_family_rivals.text: A lay follower of Augustine who wrote a book against the thirteenth Conference, without naming him.

friends_family_rivals.name: Augustine of Hippo
friends_family_rivals.text: Cassian's thirteenth Conference answered Augustine's teaching on grace, and Augustine's followers attacked it. Cassian still cites him against Nestorius, as 'the priest of Hippo'.
friends_family_rivals.source: Conference 13; On the Incarnation 7.27; Catholic Encyclopedia; Gibson
friends_family_rivals.checker 2026-09-25: No source checked says whether they met; the sentence was dropped.

friends_family_rivals.name: Nestorius
friends_family_rivals.text: Bishop of Constantinople whom he answered in seven books, calling him 'most wicked and shameless contaminator of an illustrious city'.

friends_family_rivals.name: Theophilus of Alexandria
friends_family_rivals.rel: bishop he sided with, then opposed
friends_family_rivals.text: His letter against a bodily God split the desert in 399; Cassian's side read it. Palladius names him among those who plotted Chrysostom's exile.

how_he_died.text: Nothing is recorded: no date, cause, place of death beyond Marseilles, or last words. Gennadius says only that with his book against Nestorius 'made an end, both of writing and living, at Marseilles'. He was buried at St Victor.
how_he_died.note: Later, clearly marked as later: Pope Urban V (1362-1370), once abbot of St Victor, put his head in a silver casket inscribed 'Head of St Cassian' (Orthodox Encyclopedia; Catholic Encyclopedia says 'it is related that'). The Revolution destroyed many of the abbey's relics in 1794. The head was lent to Romania in 2002.

exact_quotes.exact: and writing this, made an end, both of writing and living, at Marseilles, in the reign of Theodosius and Valentinianus

is_he_a_saint.text: Yes in the East; locally in the West. The Orthodox Church counts him a saint (Venerable, and in printed Menaia 'confessor'). The Catholic Church never canonised him formally. He was honoured at Marseilles from early on (Gregory the Great calls the women's house 'the monastery ... of Saint Cassian' in 596), but his teaching on grace kept him out of the Roman Martyrology for centuries. The current Martyrology (2004) now lists 'sancti Ioannis Cassiani' on 23 July as a local cult. The Episcopal Church remembers him on 23 July.

items.text: 29 February (28 February in other years). Called St Cassian the Roman.
Never formally canonised. In the 2004 Roman Martyrology on 23 July, marked as a local cult. Kept at Marseilles.
items.source: Martyrologium Romanum 2004; Catholic Encyclopedia ('Although never formally canonized, St. Gregory the Great regarded him as a saint'); Nominis

items.text: 23 July, 'Monastic and Theologian'. Not in the Church of England's calendar.
items.source: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022; Common Worship calendar

items.text: Not in the LCMS or ELCA commemorations.

is_he_a_saint.caveat: Gibson (1894) wrote that he was 'never formally canonized, his name is not found in the Calendars of the West; nor is he honoured with the title of Saint', and was generally called 'the blessed Cassian'. That was true of the 1916 Martyrology, but the 2004 edition now calls him 'sanctus'. The Orthodox Encyclopedia tells the long Catholic argument: condemned by some as a half-Pelagian, defended by Guesnay (1652) and the Bollandists, and settled in practice by Prospero Lambertini (later Benedict XIV), who ruled that old cults of men who argued with Augustine's disciples could not be challenged.

exact_quotes.exact: Although never formally canonized, St. Gregory the Great regarded him as a saint
Never formally canonized, his name is not found in the Calendars of the West; nor is he honoured with the title of "Saint."

prayer_he_wrote.text: Yes: the prayer that closes On the Incarnation. It is addressed to God, in his own voice.
prayer_he_wrote.exact: But, beyond and above all I pray with all my heart and voice, to Thee, O God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that Thou wouldest fill with the gift of Thy love whatever we have written by Thy bounteous grace.
prayer_he_wrote.display_full: O God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, fill with the gift of Thy love whatever we have written by Thy bounteous grace ... grant to Thy people whom Thou hast redeemed that in the Incarnation of Thine Only Begotten Son they may perceive both Thy gift and His love.
prayer_he_wrote.cite: On the Incarnation, Book 7, chapter 31 (the last paragraph)
prayer_he_wrote.note: Use the CCEL wording (Thee/Thou/Thy); New Advent modernises it to You/Your. 'display_full' is a shortened version with ellipsis and the opening turned into direct address: if printed, mark it shortened or print the whole paragraph from the CCEL file. what_to_read_first.title: The Institutes
what_to_read_first.text: Twelve short books: the monk's day, then the eight chief faults one by one. Book 10, on restlessness, reads as if written today.
what_to_read_first.note: HTTP 200, 'Institutes (John Cassian)'. Book 6 is not translated there.

what_to_read_first.title: The Conferences
what_to_read_first.text: Talks with the desert abbots. Start with Conference 1 (the goal of life) and Conference 10 (the one-line prayer).
what_to_read_first.note: HTTP 200. Conferences 12 and 22 not translated there.

what_to_read_first.title: Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 62
what_to_read_first.text: The oldest account of his life, one paragraph long, from his own city.

what_to_read_first.title: Gibson's introduction
what_to_read_first.text: Everything his writings reveal about his life, in order.

hard_topics.text: In the thirteenth Conference, Abba Chaeremon teaches that God's grace comes first and does most, but that sometimes the first stirring of a good will comes from us, and God strengthens it. Augustine's followers called this a return to Pelagius. The Council of Orange (529) rejected it, and a sixth-century list attributed to Pope Gelasius called his works 'apocryphal'. Cassiodorus told monks to read him, but carefully on free will. Defenders say he was guarding human effort against a fatalist reading of Augustine; the Orthodox Church honours him as a saint and sees no heresy in it.
hard_topics.exact: And when He sees in us some beginnings of a good will, He at once enlightens it and strengthens it and urges it on towards salvation, increasing that which He Himself implanted or which He sees to have arisen from our own efforts.
hard_topics.source: Conference 13, chapter 8; Catholic Encyclopedia, 'John Cassian' and 'Semipelagianism'; Gibson, Prolegomena
hard_topics.note: Gibson (himself an Anglican bishop) says 'a verdict of guilty must be returned', with 'a recommendation to mercy'. The Catholic Encyclopedia: 'St. Augustine regarded man in his natural state as dead, Pelagius as quite sound, Cassian as sick.'

check_extra.exact: St. Augustine regarded man in his natural state as dead, Pelagius as quite sound, Cassian as sick
check_extra.exact2: a verdict of guilty must be returned on the charge of Semi-Pelagianism in Cassian's case

hard_topics.text: Abba Joseph teaches that a lie, like a strong drug, is deadly when taken lightly but right in grave danger, and Cassian makes it his own. Augustine held that every lie is a sin.
hard_topics.exact: And so we ought to regard a lie and to employ it as if its nature were that of hellebore; which is useful if taken when some deadly disease is threatening, but if taken without being required by some great danger is the cause of immediate death.
hard_topics.note: Augustine's On Lying not fetched here.
hard_topics.checker 2026-09-25: Now checked: Augustine, Enchiridion 18 (New Advent 1302, tr. J. F. Shaw): "To me, however, it seems certain that every lie is a sin". Saved as sources/people/john-cassian/newadvent-augustine-enchiridion.txt.

hard_topics.text: He tells, as praise, of Patermucius, who entered a monastery with his eight-year-old son and, when the abbot told him to, carried the boy to the river to throw him in. Monks posted there caught the boy. Cassian says it was revealed that he had 'copied the deed of the patriarch Abraham'. Almost every reader today is horrified.
hard_topics.exact: Then he, as if this had been commanded him by the Lord, at once snatched up the child as quickly as possible, and carried him in his arms to the river's bank to throw him in.
hard_topics.note: Checked in Institutes 4.27: the boy was 'about eight years old'; 'some of the brethren' had been 'purposely set to watch the banks of the river' and snatched him out. 4.28: 'he had copied the deed of the patriarch Abraham'.

hard_topics.text: He tells how Theonas left his unwilling wife for a monastery, then insists he is not recommending divorce and is only reporting what happened.
hard_topics.exact: But let no one imagine that we have invented this for the sake of encouraging divorce, as we not only in no way condemn marriage

hard_topics.text: Against Nestorius he writes with fury: 'you most wicked and shameless contaminator of an illustrious city'. Gibson judged the book hasty and less valuable than his others.
hard_topics.exact: you most wicked and shameless contaminator of an illustrious city

extras_candidates.title: The eight thoughts
extras_candidates.text: His list of eight chief faults (gluttony, lust, greed, anger, sadness, acedia, vainglory, pride) was reworked by Gregory the Great into the seven deadly sins. The site's Christian Personality Test already builds its 'where the fight is' page on it; the sins quiz covers the same ground.
extras_candidates.note: Gregory's reworking is in his Moralia (31.45); the Gregory link is the site's own claim, checked elsewhere, not here.

hub_card.note: The hints are right. 'desert': he lived years among the desert fathers of Scete and the Delta and wrote them down. 'monks': monk and abbot. 'fathers': Church Father. Not 'teachers' (not a Doctor of the Church). 'lived': born about 360, but his works and Marseilles years are 415 to about 435, so '400s' fits. 'east west': a Latin writer in the West, venerated chiefly in the East.

checker_2026_09_25: Adversarial check of the page, 2026-09-25. Fixes beyond the items marked above:
Gennadius does NOT call him "Saint Cassianus" (Richardson's translation, chapters 62 and 85: plain "Cassianus"); the claim came off the page.

Conference 2.11: the biscuit story is told by Abba Moses, who says Serapion "used often to tell" it "to the younger brethren"; Serapion did not tell it to Cassian. He "laid it in the midst", not "on the floor".
Conference 15.3: the heretic had deceived "a large number of men" and "the simple folk of all Egypt", not "simple monks".
Institutes 5.35 names no place for Abba Theodore's visit; "Scete" was an inference (Conference 6 puts a Theodore at Cellae). The moment's place is now "Egypt".
Conference 2.5: Heron "on the third day afterward ... expired", now "on the third day".
Institutes 5.24: the fast was broken "except in the case of the regular days, Wednesdays and Fridays", now said.
Institutes 4.27: the child was thrown in ("when the child was thrown in, had somehow snatched him from the bed of the stream"), now said.
Conference 16.1: they said they were NOT brothers by birth ("a tie of spiritual and not carnal brotherhood"); the page had "They were, Cassian says, but...".
Institutes 11.18 does not say which bishop's hands; the page no longer implies it was Chrysostom (deacon by Chrysostom, priest later: Gennadius).

Orthodox Encyclopedia, 2002: Archbishop Panafieu brought the head to Romania "temporarily" for veneration and gave particles; "lent to the Romanian Church, which keeps him as a saint of the Dobruja" overstated it.
Orthodox Encyclopedia: he is the only saint with a service on 29 February "in the printed Menaia" (other saints are commemorated that day, e.g. OCA lists); now said so.
Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, p. 321: "John Cassian, Monastic and Theologian, 435", 23 July.
Roles: "Abbot" is only in the 11th-century St Victor charters; Gennadius says "a presbyter at Marseilles, founded two monasteries". The role is now "Priest".

Rule of St Benedict 42 (Verheyen): "let one read the Conferences or the Lives of the Fathers, or something else that will edify"; "the four or five pages". The number lines no longer say all 4 or 5 pages were from the Conferences.
Conference 11.4: Chaeremon was the oldest of the three (Chaeremon, Nesteros, Joseph), not the oldest abbot Cassian met; the chip is now "Chaeremon's age".
Band picture (Gallica, BnF Grec 923 fol. 30r) is not on Commons. It is a flat scan of a 9th-century page (PD-Art), but Gallica's own terms ask a fee for commercial reuse: the owner should know.

tidbits.text: The seven deadly sins were once eight. Cassian was one of the early writers who counted eight ...
tidbits.evidence: Catholic Encyclopedia (1912), 'Sin' (fetched 2026-09-25 to sources/people/john-cassian/newadvent-cathen-14004b-sin.txt, line 55): 'These are enumerated by St. Thomas (I-II:84:4) as vainglory (pride), avarice, gluttony, lust, sloth, envy, anger. ... Earlier writers had distinguished eight capital sins: so St. Cyprian (De mort., iv); Cassian (Institutes 5, Conferences 5); Columbanus ...; Alcuin .... The number seven, however, had been given by St. Gregory the Great (Lib. mor. in Job. XXXI, xvii), and it was retained by the foremost theologians of the Middle Ages.' 'One of the early lists' because the Encyclopedia names others (Cyprian, Columbanus, Alcuin). The eight in the Institutes: Catholic Encyclopedia, 'John Cassian': 'the eight remaining books are devoted to the eight principal obstacles to perfection'.
tidbits.checker: Reworded 2026-09-25 by the checker so each sentence sits on the Encyclopedia's words: 'Cassian was one of the early writers who counted eight' is its 'Earlier writers had distinguished eight capital sins: so St. Cyprian ...; Cassian ...; Columbanus ...; Alcuin'; 'The number seven comes from Gregory the Great, and the great teachers of the Middle Ages kept it' is 'The number seven, however, had been given by St. Gregory the Great ..., and it was retained by the foremost theologians of the Middle Ages.' The builder's 'kept his number' could be read as Cassian's number, and 'His Institutes are one of the early lists of eight' repeated The eight faults section.

tidbits.text: A century later, Benedict's Rule named the Conferences first ...
tidbits.evidence: Rule of St Benedict, tr. Verheyen (sources/people/john-cassian/benedict-rule-verheyen-ccel.txt). Chapter 42, line 1368: 'as soon as they have risen from their evening meal, let all sit together in one place, and let one read the Conferences or the Lives of the Fathers, or something else that will edify the hearers' ... 'All, therefore, having assembled in one place, let them say Complin'. Chapter 16, line 780: the day hours are 'Lauds, Prime, Tierce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Complin', and 'let us rise at night': eight in all. Chapter 17, line 800: at Prime 'the hymn for the same Hour be said after the verse Deus, in adjutorium (Ps 69[70]:2)', and Tierce, Sext and None 'in the same order; namely, the verse, the hymn'; chapter 18, line 827: 'In the beginning let there be said the verse, Deus, in adjutorium meum intende; Domine, ad adjuvandum me festina (Ps 69[70]:2), and the Gloria, followed by the hymn for each Hour', in the chapter that orders Prime to Complin. The night office (chapter 9) and Lauds (chapters 12 and 13) are ordered differently: hence six of eight. Abba Isaac's verse: Conference 10, chapter 10 ('O God, make speed to save me: O Lord, make haste to help me', already verified in john-cassian.quotes.json). That the Rule's 'Conferences' are Cassian's: Catholic Encyclopedia, 'John Cassian': 'St. Benedict made use of Cassian in writing his Rule, and ordered selections from the "Conferences" ... to be read daily in his monasteries.' 'A century later': the Conferences about 420 to 428 (this page), the Rule written at Monte Cassino from about 529 (Benedict's page).
tidbits.checker: Changed 2026-09-25 by the checker: 'Six of its eight hours of prayer a day open with the verse' became 'The Rule also opens most of its hours of prayer with the verse'. The count of six was our own reading. Chapter 18 opens with the verse 'followed by the hymn for each Hour' (line 827), which can be read to cover Lauds as well (seven of eight); chapter 17 gives it for Prime, Tierce, Sext and None; the night office opens otherwise (chapter 9). 'Most' holds on either reading. The Rule does not name Cassian as the verse's source, and the tidbit does not say it does: it says only that the verse is the one Abba Isaac taught him (Conference 10, chapter 10).
